title: Objectives depend on purpose and ownership

blocks.heading: Objectives depend on purpose and ownership
blocks.text: A business objective is a result the organisation seeks to achieve. Private enterprise is owned by private individuals or organisations and commonly seeks profit, survival or growth. Non-profit making activity gives priority to a social or service purpose rather than distributing profit to owners. A surplus can still be necessary to replace equipment and maintain the service. Public enterprise is owned and controlled by the state and may aim to make essential services accessible as well as cover its costs. The categories describe different aspects and can overlap: a privately organised charity can pursue a non-profit purpose. Do not classify an organisation’s purpose from its size or from one year’s financial result. A profit-seeking business that makes a loss remains profit-seeking; a non-profit organisation can record a surplus. Objectives influence decisions about prices, locations and which users are served. However, resources constrain each organisation. A service objective does not remove the need to pay workers and suppliers, and a profit objective does not prevent an owner from considering employees and the community.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Assume Tula Transport is state owned and aims to connect remote settlements. Privately owned Lika Coaches prioritises a return on its owners’ investment. Tula may retain a lightly used route to support access, while Lika may favour a more profitable route. Either operator still needs resources to maintain vehicles; different objectives explain the different choices without proving either is efficient.

blocks.heading: Non-profit making activity
blocks.text: Non-profit making activity is organised primarily to provide a social or other service benefit rather than to distribute profit to owners. It still needs income to meet costs. A surplus can be retained to sustain or improve the activity, so non-profit activity can charge fees and seek a surplus without changing its primary purpose. Success is assessed against the service objective alongside financial sustainability.
blocks.reviewed_unchanged: Re-read citing material after clarifying that non-profit services can charge fees and restating the case-specific investor condition; the remaining text is still accurate.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A community study centre charges modest fees to maintain its learning room. Charging fees does not turn its stated service purpose into a profit-distribution objective. If income exceeds costs, it can use the surplus to maintain the centre.

blocks.heading: Private enterprise
blocks.text: Private enterprise is business activity owned and controlled by private individuals or organisations rather than the state. Common objectives include profit, survival, growth and a return to owners, although private owners can also pursue social aims. A loss in one year does not change ownership or prove that the business has a non-profit purpose.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Dali Joinery is owned by two individuals who want a financial return. Their decision to buy a saw is likely to depend partly on expected sales and costs, because the stated objective is a return on their investment.

blocks.heading: Public enterprise
blocks.text: Public enterprise is owned and controlled by the state. Objectives may include providing essential services, maintaining access in less profitable areas or supporting employment, alongside meeting financial targets. State ownership does not mean that the enterprise has unlimited resources or that its customers pay nothing. Decisions must recognise both its service purpose and the cost of achieving it.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Assume Riverlink Passenger Service is state owned and tasked with serving remote settlements. A route with low ticket revenue may still serve the access objective. The enterprise must finance the route, so the benefit should be weighed against the resources it consumes.
